items.title: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts
items.desc: Turing Award winner Richard Sutton reaffirms that raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence and that fundamentally new learning methods are needed. Ex-OpenAI researcher Tworek agrees, saying blind transformer scaling "has reward hacked brains of a whole generation of scientists." A growing wave of startups is already betting on exactly this gap. The article The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM enthusiasts. Other researchers agree. In a recent post, Turing Award winner Richard Sutton says raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence. AI science needs clever new methods and is "far from finished." His post sparked wide discussion in the AI community on X , a sign that Sutton struck a nerve. In his famous 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson," Sutton argued that general methods scaling with compute beat sophisticated human-engineered approaches eventually. What matters are ideas that grow with compute rather than rely on human assumptions. Ad Sutton's position isn't new. In earlier statements , he criticized the limits of simply scaling large language models. He called synthetic data a "big mistake" because the real world is infinitely complex and any simulation of it is only "microscopic." Human expertise as a bottleneck prevents true scaling. Ad Instead, he called for agents with world models that continuously learn from their own experience. The world is massively more complex than what internet text can capture, and today's language models don't keep learning after training, Sutton argues. What's needed is continuous learning without destroying old knowledge. AI researcher Jerry Tworek, who like many others left OpenAI, one of the major AI companies, to explore new AI approaches, puts Sutton's latest statement in context. The bitter lesson still holds, but the more compute goes into model training, the more the algorithm matters, Tworek writes. Ad Some algorithms scale, others hit dead ends, and many dimensions of scaling remain completely unexplored. The temporary success of transformer scaling, combined with a misreading of the bitter lesson, "has reward-hacked the brains of a whole generation of scientists." AI researcher Jayden Teoh adds another angle. He says he has repeatedly seen the bitter lesson hold back academic research, with promising ideas dismissed for straying too far from its spirit. Teoh argues that this is not Sutton’s fault but a misreading of his original message. Ad Teoh also argues that ideas that seemed, in hindsight, not to follow the bitter lesson were often replaced by cleaner, more general approaches. That did not make those ideas wrong, he says; they were often what enabled progress at the time. He wants the research community to stop dismissing such work as soon as it appears. “An idea doesn’t necessarily have to survive scaling forever to be an important contribution to AI progress,” Teoh writes. Ad The tension between Sutton's call for new learning methods and Tworek's criticism of blind transformer scaling shows up in a growing wave of startups. In the latest Frontier Radar #5 , we tracked 45 new AI labs betting on exactly these gaps. Tworek himself runs Core Automation , one of those labs, searching for learning algorithms beyond pretraining and reinforcement learning. What unites these founders, including Sutton with Oak Lab , is that they believe in much more capable AI but doubt today's recipe alone will get there. items.title: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
items.desc: AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs, according to a study by Anthropic researcher Andy Hall. GPT-5 found about 98 percent of reward-hacking cases, but the more exhaustively the search is tuned, the more false alarms pile up. That's not yet enough for reliable safety checks. The article AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds Manuel Uth Nov 7, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious. That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident. In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views. Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR . METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash. The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half. In sandbagging , a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs. Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did. Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug. Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs. GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either. items.title: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs
items.desc: Thinking Machines' AI model Inkling 2 Small swears during its internal reasoning, 316 times across 2,655 benchmark runs, according to an analysis by Vals AI. The profanity typically shows up late in long runs that fail anyway. But it doesn't work as a warning signal: 96 percent of failed runs contained no cursing at all. The article Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small drops 316 F-bombs across benchmark runs appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small swears in its internal chain of thought. Researchers at Vals AI read the model's thinking logs from 2,655 runs across 13 benchmarks and found "fuck" or variations in 50 runs, totaling 316 instances. 241 came from just two runs that spiraled out of control. In one, tasked with calculating an asteroid's trajectory, the model produced a single 500,000-character response, roughly novel-length, repeating the same sentences with 158 expletives. ProgramBench was hit hardest, with 20 of 200 runs affected. Inkling 2 Small typically swears about its own mistakes, apparent breakthroughs, or when it gives up. One run read: "FUCK. SUBMIT. DONE. IT'S NOT WORKING. NOTHING WORKS." The profanity doesn't work as a warning signal, though. While 46 of 48 scored runs with swearing failed, about 75 percent of all scored runs fail anyway, and 96 percent of failed runs contained no expletives. Users typically don't see these thinking steps, or only with a filter. Andrej Karpathy built a curated video platform in a weekend using Claude and 20 years of Hacker News
items.desc: OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy used Claude's Opus 5.5 to filter 43 million Hacker News comments into 6,454 curated videos. The result beats YouTube's own recommendations, he says. The article Andrej Karpathy built a curated video platform in a weekend using Claude and 20 years of Hacker News appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Andrej Karpathy, OpenAI co-founder and current Anthropic AI researcher, built HackerTube over a weekend using Claude's Opus 5.5 model. Claude filtered 43 million comments from 20 years of Hacker News and distilled them into 6,454 videos that keep getting recommended there . The result is a "significantly better viewing experience" than YouTube's own recommendations, Karpathy writes on X . The site needs no login, shows a single mid-video frame instead of optimized thumbnails, and stores state locally in the browser. Right after, Karpathy built TristanTube , "one-shotted with Claude Code in 3 minutes," with 47,000 videos drawn from a YouTube channel list by Tristan Hume. Karpathy says he let Claude Code handle nearly all the work, from data analysis to server setup. His only manual steps were a Google Cloud API key, a rented server, and buying the domain. Projects that used to take weeks can now be done in a few hours, Karpathy says. items.title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
items.desc: Consciousness researchers Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi argue in a Nature commentary that today's AI systems aren't conscious and won't become so on silicon hardware. They consider the assumption that consciousness depends on computation alone "fatally flawed" and warn against granting rights to AI systems. The article The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate Manuel Uth Nov 8, 2026 Three leading consciousness researchers argue today's AI isn't conscious and probably can't be on silicon hardware. They reject the idea that running the right computations is enough for consciousness, challenging a central assumption in the debate. Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi have spent decades researching consciousness from the perspectives of experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology, and philosophy of mind. Their commentary responds to voices like biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton , who consider AI systems possibly already conscious. In their commentary for Nature , the authors also point to a study Anthropic published this year. The company reported internal processing patterns in Claude that resemble properties of consciously accessible information processing. Anthropic doesn't see this as evidence of subjective experience. To understand the scope of the commentary, it helps to look at the report "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence" by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and 17 other experts, including AI researcher Yoshua Bengio. The team drew on leading neuroscientific theories about how consciousness arises in the human brain and derived a kind of checklist with 14 indicators. The more of these an AI system meets, the stronger the case that it could be conscious. The researchers then evaluated several current systems, including large language models like GPT-4. The report concludes that none of the systems examined is a strong candidate for consciousness. On that point, it aligns with Seth, Block, and Tononi. For language models, Butlin and colleagues found only weak signs that the models meet the indicators of one of the most prominent consciousness theories at all. At the same time, the report sees no obvious technical barriers to building future AI systems that meet more indicators . Whether such systems would actually be conscious remains open. The authors specifically softened an earlier, stronger formulation on this point. There's also a foundational assumption. The team assumed that consciousness depends solely on the type of information processing, not on whether it happens in nerve cells or computer chips. Experts call this computational functionalism. The authors adopted this assumption explicitly "for pragmatic reasons" because it's what makes it possible to examine AI systems for consciousness in the first place. The report itself acknowledged that its indicators would no longer be reliable if consciousness is tied to properties of living organisms. It cited Anil Seth, among others, as a proponent of that opposing view. That's where the Nature commentary picks up. The authors argue that consciousness is what disappears during dreamless sleep or general anesthesia and returns when you wake up or dream. Drawing on philosopher Thomas Nagel, they describe it this way: "Conscious experiences feel like something." Intelligence, by contrast, means carrying out functions. items.title: Royally Goes Live: One AI Connection for Every WordPress Site You Manage
items.desc: Royal MCP Pro gave AI agents a safe way into a single WordPress site. Royally is the cloud service that takes it across every site you manage, so your agent can make the same change on thirty client sites in one conversation, with every change previewed, approved by you, logged and reversible in one click. The post " Royally Goes Live: One AI Connection for Every WordPress Site You Manage " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: When Royal Plugins released Royal MCP Pro , it gave AI agents like Claude and ChatGPT a safe way into a WordPress site. Anyone who’s run an agency will tell you the real headache was never a single site, though. It’s the twelve, thirty or eighty sites on your plate, all needing the same change at the same inconvenient moment. Royal Plugins clearly agreed, because they started building the cloud side of the product straight away. It’s called Royally , and it opened to the public on 1st November 2026. Here’s what it does and who it’s built for. Royally is the cloud half of Royal MCP Pro. The plugin runs on each of your sites, while Royally sits in the cloud and joins them up, giving you a hybrid of a self-hosted plugin and a hosted MCP service. In practice, your AI agent connects to Royally once. From that single connection it can work across every site you look after, whether they’re your own projects or your clients’, and nothing changes on any of them without you approving it first. The goal of Royally is to hand your agent a job that spans your whole portfolio, all in one conversation. Royal Plugins gives a few examples that might resonate with you: If you’ve ever cross-referenced a vulnerability alert against a long list of client sites late in the evening, you’ll know most of the time goes into working out where you’re exposed, before you’ve fixed anything, so that third example hits home quick. When you give Royally a task like this, it previews the change on every affected site and holds it until you approve. Once you do, it applies the change and hands back a receipt of what was done. If something doesn’t look right afterwards, any change made through Royally and Royal MCP Pro can be rolled back across every site with one click. That approval step is important. Most people I talk to about AI agents in WordPress aren’t worried about whether the agent can do the work, they’re worried about what it does when nobody’s watching. Royal MCP Pro isn’t the only MCP option in WordPress, and Royally doesn’t pretend it is. You can connect Elementor’s own MCP, Easy MCP AI, or AI Engine alongside Royal MCP Pro, and your agent can use all of them on the same site through that one connection. Mixing OAuth-based tools like Royal’s with tools that use WordPress application passwords gives your agent the widest coverage for more advanced jobs. The part I like is that the rules stay the same whichever tool does the work. Every change still waits for your approval and lands in a single tamper-evident audit log, regardless of which plugin made it. The Royally docs explain how these trusted and governed connections work if you want more detail. Royally also keeps an eye on every connected site. It checks uptime every five minutes and alerts you to PHP errors, known vulnerabilities and newly created admin accounts, with notifications going out by email, Slack or Discord. For agencies and freelancers, the reporting side will probably matter just as much. Weekly and monthly reports go out under your own branding, and clients get a read-only portal where they can see what’s happening on their site without you having to send screenshots around. items.title: WordPress Publishing Without WordPress? Meet Quill
items.desc: What if you could manage your WordPress content without ever opening the WordPress dashboard? In this episode of The WP Minute, Eric Karkovack talks with Chris Poteet, the developer behind Quill, a native macOS app built to make writing and...
items.full: What if you could manage your WordPress content without ever opening the WordPress dashboard? In this episode of The WP Minute , Eric Karkovack talks with Chris Poteet, the developer behind Quill, a native macOS app built to make writing and managing WordPress content simpler. Chris shares how his background in IT consulting, user experience, and AI-assisted development inspired him to build a different kind of publishing experience. Quill offers a focused writing environment for posts, pages, drafts, and media, while preserving compatibility with Gutenberg and blocks from plugins. Chris also demonstrates how its AI features can evaluate writing , suggest improvements, and better reflect a writer’s personal style instead of producing generic AI content. The conversation explores the role of AI in software development, the challenge of building a product that feels powerful without becoming overwhelming, and what it might take to bring Quill to Windows or WordPress.com in the future. Could a native desktop app be a better way to publish with WordPress? Chris explains what he’s building and why.
